idea: A Library of Congress portrait photograph of Frederick Douglass, stern and direct, captioned with his own line about learning to read: 'From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.' It comes from his 1845 Narrative, about the moment he heard his enslaver forbid anyone to teach him to read. He was the most photographed American of the 19th century, and he chose to be seen this way.

A 1906 archive photo of Mark Twain propped up in bed with his papers, captioned 'Mark Twain, at work. Not to be published for 100 years.' He dictated much of his autobiography from bed and asked that the full text wait a century after his death. The first volume came out in 2010, which makes this a shirt about patience and having the last word.

A Smithsonian photograph of the wooden hand press Benjamin Franklin is said to have worked at in London in 1726, captioned with the end of the epitaph he wrote for himself at 22: 'In a New and More Elegant Edition, Revised and Corrected, By the Author.' Franklin began his will 'I, Benjamin Franklin, of Philadelphia, printer', and for book people this joke about death is hard to beat.

A public-domain 1888 photograph of Helen Keller and Anne Sullivan, hands touching, captioned in small spaced letters 'w-a-t-e-r'. At the pump in Tuscumbia in April 1887, Sullivan spelled the word into one of Keller's hands while water ran over the other, and Keller understood that things have names. It's a quiet shirt about the moment language arrives.

An archive photograph of the masthead of the Cherokee Phoenix, printed in English and Cherokee, captioned '1821: a syllabary. 1828: a newspaper.' Sequoyah could not read any language when he created the Cherokee syllabary, and within seven years his people were printing their own newspaper, the first published by a Native American nation. It's a true story of how fast a writing system can take hold.

Mathew Brady's 1878 photograph of Thomas Edison beside his tinfoil phonograph, captioned 'phonograph (n.): Greek for sound-writing.' The name treats recorded sound as a new kind of handwriting, and the shirt shows the wearer that a machine for the ear was named after the pen.

A Library of Congress photograph of one handwritten copy of the Gettysburg Address, captioned 'Edward Everett spoke first, for two hours. This took about two.' Everett's oration ran around two hours, and Lincoln's roughly 270 words took about two minutes. It's a shirt for anyone who believes in cutting.

An archive photo of a newspaper pressman in the square paper hat that pressmen folded from a sheet of newsprint to keep ink out of their hair, captioned 'Made from today's paper.' It's a real print-shop custom, a small origami crown made of the news itself, for anyone who knows the craft or likes clever hats.

The famous photograph of Walt Whitman with a butterfly perched on his finger, captioned 'Self-published. Self-reviewed. (The butterfly is cardboard.)' Whitman paid for the 1855 Leaves of Grass himself and anonymously wrote glowing reviews of it, and the die-cut cardboard butterfly from the photo is now in the Library of Congress. It's a sly, affectionate shirt about writers building their own legend.

A close-up archive photograph of the title page of Noah Webster's 1828 An American Dictionary of the English Language, captioned 'colour → color. centre → center. Argument ongoing.' Webster used his dictionary to push American spellings that set the language on two tracks. It's a good-looking spelling fight for editors on both sides of the Atlantic.

A Library of Congress portrait photograph of journalist Ida B. Wells, captioned 'Memphis, 1892. They destroyed her press. She kept publishing.' A mob wrecked the office of her newspaper Free Speech after she wrote about lynching, and that same year she published Southern Horrors from New York. It's a shirt that sides with the press and with nerve.

An archive photograph of a young speller at an early National Spelling Bee, standing at the microphone, captioned '1925. Winning word: gladiolus.' Eleven-year-old Frank Neuhauser won the first national bee with that word. It's a sweet, specific shirt for word kids, past and present.

A close-up photo of a schoolchild's Palmer Method practice sheet filled with rows of looping ovals and push-pull strokes, no letters at all, captioned 'Before the letters, the ovals.' American schools drilled these arm-movement exercises for decades, and the page reads like an abstract drawing. It's for anyone who believes that practice comes before style.

A Smithsonian photograph of a page from the Jefferson Bible, with cut-out columns of Greek, Latin, French and English pasted side by side, captioned 'Edited with a razor. Thomas Jefferson, c. 1820.' Jefferson cut up copies of the Gospels to keep Jesus's moral teachings and leave out the miracles. It's a shirt about strong opinions and serious editing.

A National Postal Museum photograph of a small WWII V-Mail letter, handwriting shrunk to a photographic print, captioned 'Love letter, microfilmed. 1942–45.' Letters were photographed onto film, shipped overseas and printed again at the other end, so a single sack of film replaced 37 mailbags of paper. It's a tender, clever image of words made small enough to travel.

An archive photograph of a box of John Thoreau & Co. pencils, captioned 'Henry David Thoreau, pencil maker.' Before and after Walden, Thoreau worked in his family's pencil business and improved how its graphite was made. It's a surprising, true fact for writers who know that tools come before words.

A tight archive photograph of the carved words 'FREE TO ALL' over the entrance of the Boston Public Library's 1895 McKim building, with no caption. Boston's was the first large free public library in a US city, and the three words carved in stone make a calm, permanent position on who books are for.

The 1864 Brady studio photograph of Abraham Lincoln reading to his son Tad, captioned 'Father and son, reading. (It was a photo album.)' The famous image was copied for years as Lincoln reading the Bible to his boy, but historians say the book was one of the studio's photograph albums. It's a warm picture with a wink about how myths get printed.

An archive photograph of a lector seated on a high platform reading a newspaper aloud above rows of cigar rollers in Tampa, captioned 'El lector. Paid by the workers, to read to the workers.' Cigar makers chipped in from their wages to hear news, politics and novels read while they worked. As the story goes, Montecristo cigars are named after a favourite book.

A Matson Collection photograph (Library of Congress) of a scribe in Jerusalem writing a Torah scroll with a quill, captioned '304,805 letters. Every one by hand. Every one checked.' A Torah scroll is not fit for use if even one letter is missing or extra until it is fixed. It's a shirt about the kind of care no spellcheck can give.
